titleStmt.title: Interview with Joseph Bernard Rose, 11/11/2013

bibl.title: Interview with Joseph Bernard Rose
bibl.author: Ari Fisz and Jean M. Tartaglia [transcriber]

projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Joseph Bernard Rose was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Today is November 11, 2013. I am the interviewer, Ari Fisz; and this morning I am speaking with Joseph Rose.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Mr. Rose, what's your date of birth?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: 2 January, 1919.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: 2 January of 1919. He is a veteran of the Unites States Navy. And when was the beginning of your service, sir?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: 3rd July, 1940.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: 1940. And then the end of your service.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: 1 August, 1970.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: And beginning time of the interview, I have 10:07 a.m. All right. Now, as far as the parties who are present, we have Mr. Rose, myself, and the court reporter. And I am with the Lake County State's Attorney's Office. Now, we mentioned, sir, that you were in the Navy; is that right.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: And from 1940 through 1970, obviously, you were enlisted during several wars; is that correct?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: I went through II, Korean and Nam.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Word World II, Korean and Vietnam?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: And what rank did you attain while you were in the service, sir?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: I was a master chief petty officer.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: And during--and this is going to be kind of a broad question--but from 1940 to 1970, what are the different places in the world where you served?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: San Francisco to Hong Kong, Adak, Alaska to Sydney, Australia.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Wow! Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: I can't be--

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: No. That's amazing. That's great.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Guam, Philippines, Nam.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Now, I'll start sort of in the beginning. Were you drafted or did you enlist.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Oh, no. No. I enlisted.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: And why did you choose to enlist?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Why? Well, first of all, there were no jobs '38, '39 and '40. I was tired of running around down on the farmland of Northern Illinois. And the draft was just getting ready to start and ready to grab me so I went in the Navy.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: You said Northern Illinois. Where are you from?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Do you know where Ottawa is, Starved Rock?

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Yes. That's where you're from?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay. Born and raised?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Born and raised there.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Born and raised. And why is it that you chose the Navy as opposed to some other branch?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: I didn't like carrying that Springfield rifle, the 42-pound pack, on my back.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay. Now, do you recall your first days of service.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: What do you want to know?

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: I want to know, generally, what you remember about it, what it felt like.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Well, I joined the Navy. I shipped in in Chicago, in the old post office building.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Post office building?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: And they didn't have room. That's when they were expanding the--starting to expand.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: They didn't have room for us in Great Lakes, so they put us up in a hotel for a week.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Oh, yeah?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: I spent the first week in the Navy. I was in a hotel and eating in Thompson's restaurants in Chicago, Illinois.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay. Was joining the Navy something that you had thought of in your younger years, that it might be possible for you, or was it just a surprise that just came along.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Well, the war was coming up, and there's no work down there in that farmland unless you're a farmer.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: So I just thought I'd go.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: You started in Chicago. Did you have some type of boot camp or training experience early on?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: No. No. I had no military experience whatsoever until I joined the Navy.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: And then after you enlisted, there was some type of training, I assume?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Wait a minute. Well, I went through boot camp here at Great Lakes.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Here in Great Lakes, here in Lake County?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: What was that like?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: It wasn't too bad because it was all brand new.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Do you remember anything in particular--do any of your instructors sort of stand out, anything you remember in that vein?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Well, I had a chief gunner's mate as a drill instructor.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Oh, yeah!

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: An old chief gunner's mate.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Anything in particular about him you remember?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: No. He just ran us around was all.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: How long did that last, boot camp?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: God! I don't know. I think we were--I know I--about eight, ten weeks, 12 weeks. I don't know. I don't remember. Someplace around there.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay. Something like that. And then where did you go after that.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: I went to San Pedro Harbor and went aboard the USS Colorado for transportation to Pearl.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: And USS Colorado, that was the ship, I think, you spent a lot of time on; is that right?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: I spent a little over two years on it.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Two years. And you said "Pearl." That's Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Well, I--there's a whole raft of us left here at the time. So we were all assigned to Concord DESPAC out in Pearl, commander cruise destroyers force in Pearl.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: So when you boarded the ship in Colorado, you were headed out towards Pearl Harbor; is that right?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: We were put aboard there for transportation. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: But the old man, he decided, well, he--instead of having--well, they all ran a short crew, and he decided to keep us. He had us, so he just kept us.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay. And do you remember when you arrived in Pearl Harbor, what year?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Well, we played around--

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Let me ask it, actually, a better way: Were you there before the attack or after the attack, Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Pearl Harbor was December 7th of 1941, I think.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: No. I wasn't there. Where was I? December 7th. I know I made third class the 1st of December in--oh, I know I was--I was up in--we were up in the Navy yard in Bremerton, Washington.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: In Washington?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: What were you doing there?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Well, the ship went in for a major overhaul.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: And we had been in dry dock, and we had just completed--we had completed our work in the dock and we were on trial run down to Puget Sound. And this sounds funny, but the fire room caught afire. You know, a natural fire in the actual fire room.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Oh, wow!

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Killed six men.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Oh, my God!

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: And we turned around and we went back in. And they put us right back in dry dock because they says, well, we just finished everything we were going to do. So that's when they were coming out with these new automatic weapons, like the 40 millimeter, the 20 millimeter. And so we got all that stuff on.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Then they did the other work that they were going to do.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: After the overhaul was complete, where did you sail to then?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: We went down to San Francisco, and from there we went out to Pearl.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Let's see. I have to stop and think. Yeah. We were out there. Let's see. Corral Sea come around about that time, and we were out southeast of--or southwest of Pearl, out there someplace between--not at the battle, but out in that area. We come back to San Francisco. And about that time, we went up north between the Aleutian Islands and Midway--the Battle of Midway. And when that was over with, we come back to San Francisco. And from there we went on out to Pearl.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: So you and your ship were involved in the Battle of Midway?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: We were the force that was standing between the battle and the mainland in case the Japanese kicked the hell out of us out there. They came in on the main land.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay. I see. Let me ask you then, while we're talking about battles: During World War II was your ship and you involved in any battles?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: The Colorado went through the war and--

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: For the record, Mr. Rose has just handed me his belt buckle. On the front of it it reads: USS Colorado BB-45 1923 through 1947, and the belt buckle reads: USS Colorado Alumni Association. And then on the back, it has a list of combat areas. The first one is--I'm going to mess up the pronunciations--Tarawa.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Tarawa. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Tarawa, T-a-r-a-w-a. And then the second one is Kwajalein.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Kwajalein.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Kwajalein which is K-w-a-j-a-l-e-i-n. Then Eniwetok.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Eniwetok.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: E-n-i-w-e-t-o-k.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yeah. The old Marshalls group. Marshalls-Gilberts.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: And then Saipan, Guam, which is S-A-I-P-A-N, Guam. And then Tinian.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Tinian.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: T-i-n-i-a-n. Then you have Leyte, Mindoro. L-e-y-t-e and Mindoro, M-i-n-d-o-r-o. And then Luzon, L-u-z-o-n, and Okinawa, O-k-i-n-a-w-a. So you have eight combat areas.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: You know, I wasn't on there during all of that because I left in--I picked up another new--I come back to the States, picked up new construction, the small one. I looked at it and I thought: Man, I'll never get more than 25 miles off of the coast, 160 feet long and 25 feet wide.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Yeah. Are there any of those combat areas that you were involved in that stand out in your mind?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: No. Okay. Any particular experiences in that vein that would stand out in your mind.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: No. Okay. You--that belt buckle read 1923 through 1947 for the USS Colorado. Is that your personal--Well, no. That would have been before your personal involvement with the Colorado. So the Colorado was sort of done in action in 1947?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Oh, yeah. She was--1947 they chopped her up, and you probably--well, you're too young to do it, but we were shaving with it.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Oh, yeah!

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Well, they chopped it up, sold it for scrap.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay. So what did you do after your time in World War II? You were involved in Korea, as well?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yeah, I come back to the--let's--

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: World War II ended in '45; right?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yeah, '45.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: And Korea was '53?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: '53, something like that.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: So what happened in those eight years that are in the interim?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Well, one of the things that happened, I got involved in the training command.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: In what kind of command?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: In the training command.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Training command.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Where you--I had to teach people how to shoot guns in World War II.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: You know, they bring people in, and north of San Diego out by La Jolla--

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: --in Pacific Beach, California--well, there's two Pacific Beaches. One is up around San Francisco, and this one was down around La Jolla. And they--right on the oceanfront they built this anti-aircraft training center.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: And they take people in there, put them on the guns, teach them how to shoot, how to maintain them. And then they send them out to the fleet.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: And you were one of the teachers or trainers?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: And I come back in 1945. I spent--I don't know--about a month, part of it, at the naval pier down in Chicago.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: They had a big receiving station down there, and that's where they sent people. And I got orders to that, and I went to the anti-aircraft training center in Pacific Beach. I was there about--I don't know--about possibly six months, and they disestablished it and they moved us aboard ship. They gave us a cruiser to--it was an anti-aircraft training ship. So we'd take people aboard ship, put them on the guns, take them out and fire them. And I did that for quite a while.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Quite a while.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay. Well, let's move on to Korea then. What involvement did you have during the Korean War.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: I went aboard the USS Ajax which is a repair ship.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: And we left--it was in San Diego. When I went aboard, we left there, went out to Japan. And we were--we'd go out--go out and run around for a little while. It was a repair ship. Of course, we couldn't do anything out at sea. I mean, no repairs out at sea. But when we was in port, we might have six or eight ships aboard side for repair. They could do anything on that ship. This ship was nothing but a massive big machine shop.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay. So a repair ship would--

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: USS Ajax.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: USS Ajax. And this ship would help other ships that needed various repairs?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yeah. Anything that they needed done we could do.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: But we didn't stay in port all the time. We'd go out and run around, and then come back, tie up.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Since it was a repair ship, I'm guessing there was never any combat that you saw while you were on that ship or is that wrong?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: No. We went over and ran up and down the coast of Korea. But, you know, the old man, he had to go out to sea.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: When you say "the old man," what do you mean?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Captain.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: The captain. Okay. You said he had to go out to sea?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Well, you know, you can't stay in port all the time.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay. Are there any experiences during the Korean War that stand out in your mind?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: You said you were involved in--your service went through such that it included Vietnam, as well; is that right?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: And how would you describe your involvement in that conflict?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Well, the detailer, the guy that makes assignments, was a chief petty officer that I knew, and he and I had done duty together. I was here at Great Lakes. And he come in and we were sitting around talking. He says: I got a good ship for you. I says: Why can't I stay here? Because I had to go to sea and then come back, and I was going to twilight. Well, the last two years are your twilight cruise on 30 years, and I was going to do that here because my family was here. My wife was in school teaching, and my son was starting to go to school. And I couldn't pick them up, take them out to San Diego where the ship was home ported and get them established before we left because the detailer told me that--he lied to me. He said they were going to be here all of the time that I needed to finish off my two years at sea. So I went to San Diego, went aboard ship, ten days later we were on our way to Nam.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: And you didn't know that that was going to happen?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Was that unusual or was that common?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Well, no. I mean, it can happen. It's just one of those things that happens in life.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: And I went aboard ship. I spent the two years standing up in an eight-inch turret with a firing key in my hand. A friend of mine--I didn't know him at the time--he was--we both belonged to a club out here, and he was in there talking with some people. And I heard him. And he was mentioning something that was going on when he was in the--he was a corpsman with the Marines.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: And he was over in Nam, and he was talking about this cruiser sitting offshore firing; and every once in a while we'd drop one right in the middle of where they were. And I got talking with him, and I'm the guy that was shooting at him.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Really!

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: And we laugh about it.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: He and I turned out to be pretty good friends.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: You mentioned your wife and your son. What year did you get married, if you don't mind my asking?

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: The year that the Korean War began?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yeah. I was going to school in Washington, D.C.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: At one time the Navy had--all of the schools that they had were back in Washington, and I had been trying to get to school. And I finally got lucky; and I hit it; and I went back to gunner's mate school. And while I was running around back there trying to learn gunnery, I met my wife and convinced her she should go to California with me.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: That would have been D.C. then that you met your wife?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay. And you convinced her to go back to California with you?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: She was--it's funny how--she married out because she is Pennsylvanian Dutch.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: And if you'd been back in Pennsylvania or down in Southern, Illinois, where the Pennsylvanian Dutch are, you'd been around them, they may be--people may say they're strange. But they have their own ways, but they're real good people.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: And they didn't recognize us for the first ten years we were married?

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Really!

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Because I'm an outsider.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: You mean her family didn't recognize the two of you as a married couple for the first ten years?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Most of them.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Was there something special that happened at the end of the ten years that made them start to recognize you or they just sort of--

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Well, we had the son.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: That will do it. So your son was born in--

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Oh, no. No. He was born in Evanston, Illinois.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: What year?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Oh, I wish you hadn't asked me that!

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Oh, no. No. No. '59, I think.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: '59. Yeah. '59, right around in there because we left Washington, D.C., went to California. I went aboard ship. And when I come back, I had my orders to go--I came back here, I think. Anyway, I know I was in Illinois at Northwestern University ROTC.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: And he was born there. And then we went--Where did we go? I guess we went back out to California. I spent all of my time out in California.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Where in California?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: San Diego.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: San Diego.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: So when you were away, when you were at sea, how did you stay in touch with your wife and your son?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Writing letters.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Writing letters?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: And your wife would write you back letters?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: How often would you say that you received letters from her?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Oh, she was pretty good at that. She was pretty good at writing. I'd get at least a letter a week.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: A letter a week?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: And then what about you, you wrote letters back, as well, about how often, would you say?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Well, I would write them in--if we were out at sea, we might be out a month or so. Write a letter and drop it in the mailbox, and they would sit there. And then when we got back in port, we'd transferred it off of ship.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: So she may get four, five or six letters all at the same time.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Right. Because they couldn't be sent off until you pulled into a port; is that right?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay. Now, your boy would have been--as you got towards the tail end of your Navy career, your boy would have been eight, nine, ten, 11 years old. The way that you stayed in touch with him at that time, also, was by way of letter?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay. As far as children, you have one child then.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay. Any grandchildren?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: I have four granddaughters.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Four granddaughters?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: So your son has four daughters?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Does he live around here? Is he local?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: He's over in Ohio. He's over in Warren, Ohio.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: What does he do for a living?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: I wish you hadn't asked me that. No. He works for a company that--he's a chemist, and he--they take blood out of people and get all of the stuff out of it that they make medicine out of.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Wow! Smart guy, huh?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Well, yeah. He's pretty smart.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: All right. Let's see here. You were out at sea either during World War II or the Korean War or the Vietnam War for long periods at a time.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: I have 24 out of 30 years aboard ship.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: 24 out of 30 years?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay. What did you do for entertainment while you were out on the ship?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Well, depending upon the ship, but--well, we played poker a little bit.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Played poker.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: A little bit. Whatever else--whatever we could do to entertain ourselves is what we did.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay. Do you recall anything--any events that were particularly unusual or funny, humorous, anything like that, while you were out on the ships with your ship mates.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Well, you know, what we think is funny and what is humorous to us aboard ship, like that, people look at us, if we mention it, and they shake their head and they say: There's something wrong with you people enjoying stuff like that. But, no. Oh, we played cards. We had movies.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Oh, yeah?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. We had a movie--well most every day.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Really!

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Were there a lot of movies that were out or released back then? You know, like how it is now, there's--you know, ten movies come out every week?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Well, yeah. There's--they would pick up the movies. And then if we happen to run into another ship out at sea, we'd--one of the things we'd transport back and forth would be movies. We'd swap. What movies you got? And we'd swap them back and forth, get new movies.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay. Were the movies military in nature--

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: --or was it just actual Hollywood movies?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Regular movies.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Oh, yeah, we had learning--or the--

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Training?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Training movies. Yeah, we had them. And you always had--well, I was--they did away--when they made pay grades E8 and 9 in the Navy, they did this because they had done away with warrant officers in the Navy. And eight and nine were made to fill that blank. And that's what I was. I was--and we--well, like a ship's gunner. I had the gunnery. I had the gunners' mates and the equipment, and that's what we did.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Oh, okay. Now, you attained the rank of master chief; is that correct?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Again, I'm sorry for being naive about this. But as I understand it, that's a very high rank; is that correct?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: That's the highest enlisted rank in the Navy.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: And when is it that you attained that rank?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: I made seven in '57--or wait a minute. Well, I made nine in '62. I was eight years--my last eight years I was an E9.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: And does an E9--does that mean master chief?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Uh-huh. That was master chief.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: And how is it that your duties changed once you became a master chief?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Well, when you--There is nothing in civilian life equivalent to a chief petty officer in the Navy or a sergeant major in the Army. My--well, my duties were mostly training. I had anything from--depending upon the ship you're on--I had five men on one ship. And I got aboard an aircraft carrier, and I had 20.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: What did you mean, Joe, when you said there's no equivalent in civilian life of being a chief petty officer? What do you mean when you say that?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: I don't think that--I've been running around now since 1970 as a civilian. And I have a lot of people--well, a lot of people I know, civilian friends now. And being around in civilian life more than the military, you people don't live the way we do. I mean, civilian life is different than military life. Well, it has to be.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Which would you say--you spent 30 years in military life; yes?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: And then civilian life after that would have been 43 years?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: I'm out over 40 years.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Over 40 years. So you spent 30 in military life and 40 in civilian life. I don't know if this is a question that you can answer, but which did you prefer? Which were you more comfortable with? How is that for a question?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: When I was in the military, I was in the military; and I had a lot of civilian friends. When I was in San Diego, I lived out in a community where the majority of people out there were involved with the military one way or another. But they were all civilians--a lot of them were civilians. And back here--when I come back here, very--well, there's military here, but I lived over in the civilian community.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Do you recall--your service ended in 1970; is that right?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Do you recall the actual day that your service ended? I don't mean the date. I mean, as you think back, can you remember your last day in the Navy?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Oh, yeah!

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: What do you remember about that?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Well, they--I was down here at Great Lakes, and I was in the security department down there. I was a base armor. I had the armory down there which has--well, basically, the people--at that time we used to fire the gun salutes. And we had ammunition magazines down on the waterfront. At one time down here at Great Lakes--people don't realize it--but they had a gunnery school down there that they fired down there into the lake.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Didn't know that.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: And they've removed them, but down on the waterfront they used to have--when I first came here--there were no guns down there; but they had the base ringers for the mounts on the ground.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: And there were a couple of buildings that they used as ammunition magazines down there. They were still there. Well, we used them.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: But--

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Well, what happened on your last day of service?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Well, the old man called me in. Well, I went up, and they had a retirement ceremony. There were--three of us retired at the same time.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: And he just give us the usual talk about our service, you know, and handed us our discharge.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Now, you were--what year did you say you were born?

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: 1919. So you would have been 51 years old at the time that you retired from the Navy; is that right?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay. And you said that happened up here at Great Lakes.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Now, what did you do in the days and weeks and months after your retirement from the Navy?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Well, I come home and the wife says--when we came home, the wife says: What are you going to do now? And I said: Coffee klatch with the neighbor ladies. And she says: No. You're not. Get a job.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Where was home at the time?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: It was here in Waukegan.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: In Waukegan?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: That's where your wife and son were living at the time?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yeah. She was teaching school. Son was in school.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: And so I had been going to school off and on all during the time I was in the service. So I took the entrance exams up at Carthage.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Carthage College?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Uh-huh. I went up to Carthage for two years and finished off my degree in elementary education.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Oh, okay!

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: And taught school for 20 years.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Taught school for 20 years?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Taught school where; somewhere around here?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Which school?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: You know where Immaculate Conception is over on Grand Avenue?

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: I taught there for 20 years.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Immaculate Conception?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: For 20 years. From when to when?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Something like that.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay. And what did you teach there?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Fifth grade.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Fifth grade?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: The whole time, all 20 years you taught fifth grade?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: How did you enjoy that experience?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: The kids didn't learn a darn thing, but I had a lot of fun.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: I'm sure they learned plenty. Was Immaculate Conception kindergarten through fifth grade or did it go all the way up through junior high and high school?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: It goes up to eighth grade.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: To eighth grade?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay. So then you retired from teaching sometime in the early '90s; is that right?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: And that was your retirement, retirement? You were done working then; is that right?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yes, in a way. I got involved with the literacy program out at CLC.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: And I work in that.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: When did you get involved in the literacy program, ballpark?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: About '92, '93, '94, back in there.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: And how long did you work with the literacy program?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: I'm still.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Still doing it?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay. And how old are you today, sir?

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: 94. And you're still working with the literacy program?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yeah. Why not? I have to do something.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: No. I know.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: I can't--you cannot chase girls 24 hours a day. It's a lot of fun, and it's worth trying; but you can't do it.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Can't do it. It's exhausting. You know, when you say you still work with the literacy program today, what kind of work do you do with the literacy program?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: I tutor. I do mostly math.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Tutor, like, high school kids or younger than that?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: It's mostly adults.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Adults?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Uh-huh. People who have dropped out of school and come back because they know they have to have an education and they're trying to get a new job or people who are trying to get a--maybe working on a degree and they need a little bit of help.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay. Do you belong to any veterans' organizations?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yes. I belong to Fleet Reserve.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Fleet Reserve?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: And what type of an organization is that?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: We're all retired military. Army, Navy-- Well, no, not the Army. Navy, Marine Corps and Coast Guard.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: You said you got married in '53; was it?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: And how long were you married?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: My wife died in '90--about 1990, something like that.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Oh, man. Okay. And you haven't remarried since?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: You have remarried?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Oh, sure.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: When did you get remarried?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: She'd shoot me. Well, '92, I think.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: '92 and still married today?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: No, she passed away. I'm hard on woman. I've gone through two wives. She passed away '90, '91.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay. And did you have any children from your second marriage?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: No. No. No.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Just the one son you have?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: When I got married the second time, I was-- well, Helen was up in her upper '70s and I was in my upper '70s, low '80s.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay. I see.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: So we're just--

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Yeah. I missed my math there. Sorry about that. Do you--you know, based on your--I'm asking you some personal questions now, but let me go back to the military issue. Did your military experience influence your thinking about subjects like war or the military in general.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Well, you know, if somebody is trying to play around with us and cause us trouble, I think we should take care of them.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: That's a fair point.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Get rid of them. And then we don't have to worry about them.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: And would you say that was your sort of way of thinking when you first joined the Navy back in 1940?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Probably not.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Probably not. What would you say your way of thinking in that respect was back then, if you even really thought about that type of issue?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Never thought about it.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: You were a young man then, 21, I think?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: I was 21 when I entered the service.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay. You said that you were involved during World War II, the Korean War and the Vietnam War. Were there any big differences between your experiences from one war as compared to the other.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Well, yeah. My experiences differed because I started out down here, and I wound up up here. And you're learning how to handle stuff, how to take care of your equipment, make sure it works. As you grow up, instead of being more of a worker, you're more of an administrator.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: And I had more and more people working for me because I had more and more--well, you might say you get--as you grow up, you have more responsibility.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: So would you say then that your experience during any one of the wars was more difficult for you personally as compared to any of the others? I mean, I would think, you know, during World War II, you, obviously, had a lower rank than you did in the Korean War or the Vietnam War.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Did the fact that you had a lower rank mean that that experience for you in that war was more difficult for you in any way than it would have been in the later wars?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: No. Just different, not necessarily more difficult?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Just different. I was doing the same thing.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: I mean, I've been involved with a gun all my life.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: You've been--I didn't hear you. You've been what?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: I've been involved with a weapon all my life.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay. Even as you were in the higher ranks?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yeah. That's all I did.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: All I did was take care of weapons.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: That was your specialty?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yeah. I'm a gunner's mate.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: How is that defined, a gunner's mate?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Well, just that. I had to take care of weapons and ammunition and all of the equipment that goes with it.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay. And did you have any experience with weapons or weaponry before you enlisted in the Navy in 1940.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Well, I was a kid running around on the farm, and I had rifle.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Right. Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: And my dad had a couple pistols and I--

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: But, obviously, you learned quite a bit in the Navy about that topic?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Well, I went in the Navy and I got in the gunnery department and gunnery division, and that's all I've ever done. I mean, that's been my work all my life in the service.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: When you retired in 1970, did you--Since you'd spent 30 years dealing with weapons and guns and that sort of thing, do you still, like, go out and shoot now?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: I don't do much shooting anymore, but I still have a couple weapons.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: But earlier on--I guess, early years after your retirement from the military in the '70s, '80s, that sort of thing, I would guess you would go out and shoot, hunt, stuff like that?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: I taught my son how to handle a gun.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: You did?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: They were in the house, and all kids are curious.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: So I made sure he knew what it was and what it could do.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: That's good.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: And so he has his weapons now.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: And you said he's got four daughters?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: And I asked you about grandchildren. And I didn't ask you about great grandchildren. Are there any great grandchildren?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Not from him, but from--my wife has got children, grandchildren and great grandchildren all through this area.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Your first wife?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: No, second wife.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Second wife. okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: The only children my first wife had was by me.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Right. And what's your boy's name? What's your son's name?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: John.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: John. As we sort of get towards the end of, at least the questions that I have here, how would you say--this is a very general question--but how would you say that your service in the military and your experiences in the military affected your life?

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: Well, just like your experiences have affected your life and like your experiences have affected yours. I probably look at life a little bit different than what you do because my life has been entirely different than yours.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: But I've been around people all my life, associated with people, and I've worked with my hands all my life. I'm what you'd call a dirty hands person. I've worked with my hands all my life.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: And so I don't think there's anything wrong with working. I like it.

sp.speaker: Ari Fisz
sp.p: That's good.

sp.speaker: Joseph Bernard Rose
sp.p: For the record, it's 11:02 a.m.; and our interview with Mr. Rose has concluded.
